prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.match: Sensitive information reaches a recipient who should not receive it
An API lets a user read or change individual object fields they should not

pairs.item: Information exposure through an error message
pairs.match: An error response reveals details about users, data or the environment
Refusing a protected action when the permission check cannot be completed

explanation: Use the term that identifies the failure being discussed.

prompt: A profile page shows only the user's name and course, but the API response behind it also contains the user's password-reset token. What is the right assessment?

options.text: It's exposed; remove it from the response on the server
No problem, because the page never displays the token to users
options.why: Anyone can read the full response in developer tools, even if the page hides it.

options.text: Hide the token with CSS so it cannot be seen on the page
options.why: CSS only hides it on screen; the token is still in the response.

options.text: Encode the token with Base64 before it is returned to the page
options.why: Base64 is reversible encoding; the token is still exposed.

explanation: Browser developer tools, another client or a saved download can expose what the page never shows. Assess what the server sends, not what the page displays.

prompt: Complete the checks for deciding whether a property belongs in an API response.
text: [[Need|Speed|Format]]: does this response function require the property? [[Audience|Cost|Version]]: which user or client receives it? [[Permission|Popularity|Encoding]]: may that recipient read this property?
explanation: Define what each endpoint returns for each audience, and leave out anything that fails one of these checks.

prompt: Why use an explicit response model rather than returning the whole object and removing a list of known secrets?

options.text: Newly added internal fields won’t leak out by accident
Explicit models make API responses noticeably faster
options.why: Explicit models aren't about speed; they control which fields are allowed out.

options.text: Removing fields from a response isn't allowed by HTTP
options.why: HTTP doesn't forbid removing fields; the issue is new fields slipping through a blocklist.

options.text: Explicit models encrypt the response automatically
options.why: Response models select fields; they don't encrypt anything.

explanation: Selecting the intended properties makes the public representation easier to understand and review.

prompt: A front-end display condition enforces which fields a recipient may see.
explanation: Link response shaping to the server's access policy. The client still receives whatever the server sends.

prompt: Match each error-response detail to what it may disclose.

pairs.match: File paths, framework structure and implementation details
Table names, query structure or fragments of stored data
Whether a particular account or identifier exists
Configuration, local variables or environment details

explanation: A useful public error can be concise while internal diagnostics stay restricted.

prompt: A booking fails because the database is unavailable. Which public error response is most appropriate?

options.text: "We could not complete that request. Reference: 4F7K."
"SQLException: connection refused at db01:5432 in BookingRepo.java:118"
options.why: This exposes the database host, port and source file, which helps an attacker.

options.text: "Booking failed for jo@example.com: table bookings locked"
options.why: This reveals a user's email address and internal table details.

options.text: A blank page with HTTP 200
options.why: A blank page with a success code hides the failure and gives the user nothing to report.

explanation: A short message with an opaque reference lets staff find the detailed diagnostic record, which stays restricted. Also check whether the failed operation left an unintended change behind.

prompt: Sign-in returns "Password is incorrect" for a real account and "No account with that address" for an unknown one, both with the same HTTP status. What is the issue?

options.text: The two different messages reveal which accounts exist
No issue, because both responses use the same HTTP status
options.why: Attackers read the message body, not only the status code, so different wording still leaks.

options.text: It shows credential stuffing has already succeeded
options.why: The messages reveal which accounts exist, not that any password has been guessed.

options.text: It is a cross-site scripting flaw in the sign-in form
options.why: No script is being injected; the problem is the information the messages give away.

explanation: An account list supports phishing and password attacks, but it does not prove the attacker knows any passwords.

prompt: Both failed sign-ins now show "Unable to sign in with those details", but unknown usernames are rejected immediately while real ones go through costly password verification. What fixes this?

options.text: Make both failures do similar password-checking work, so timing matches
Reword the message again so it gives even less information
options.why: The words are already identical; the leak is the time each failure takes.

options.text: Return HTTP 404 for unknown users and HTTP 401 for real ones
options.why: Different status codes would leak account existence even more directly.

options.text: Show a CAPTCHA only when the sign-in is for a real account
options.why: A CAPTCHA only for real accounts would itself reveal which accounts exist.

explanation: A repeatable timing difference is an account-existence clue. One slow response proves nothing, because network delay and load also affect timing.

prompt: Adding a file to .gitignore removes it from the repository's committed history.
explanation: Ignore rules concern files that are not already tracked. Earlier snapshots still contain the committed content.

prompt: An API key was committed to a repository and pushed. Which action stops the key itself from working?

options.text: Revoke or rotate the key
Delete the file containing the key in a new commit
options.why: The key stays in earlier commits and in any copies people already have.

options.text: Add the file containing the key to .gitignore
options.why: .gitignore only affects untracked files; the committed key is still there.

options.text: Rewrite the repository history to remove the file
options.why: Rewriting history doesn't invalidate the key, and copies may already exist.

explanation: Deleting a secret does not invalidate it, and cleaning history cannot retrieve copies already downloaded. Revoke or rotate, investigate for use of the key, and clean history as separate steps.

prompt: Match each action to what it achieves.

pairs.match: Replaces the credential and retires the previous value
Reduces future exposure but cannot retrieve copies already downloaded

explanation: Applications that need the replacement credential must be updated after rotation.

prompt: With directory listings turned off, visitors can still fetch files from an exposed .git folder if they know the file names.
explanation: Directory listings being off does not prevent requests for known filenames. Deploy only intended files and deny Git paths.

prompt: Before exporting private records, the application checks permission. Match each result to the correct behaviour.

pairs.why: Permission was granted, so the export can proceed.
Permission was refused, so the export must not happen.

pairs.match: Refuse for now and report the problem
pairs.why: An unavailable checker hasn't granted permission, so fail closed.

explanation: This is failing closed: an unavailable checker has not granted permission. Make the decision before releasing the records.

prompt: A response contains sensitive account data. What should its caching policy do?

options.text: Stop it being stored anywhere, for example with `Cache-Control: no-store`
Cache it for as long as possible to reduce load on the server
options.why: Caching sensitive data means copies can be served to the wrong person later.

options.text: Nothing, because caching a response can't cause a disclosure
options.why: Shared or browser caches can hand a stored copy to someone else.

options.text: Nothing, because HTTPS already stops caches keeping a copy
options.why: HTTPS encrypts transit; it doesn't stop browsers or proxies keeping a copy.

explanation: Cached representations can stay available beyond their intended use. Cache policy complements, but does not replace, access control.

prompt: A profile response contains a recovery token the recipient should not receive. A developer adds context-aware HTML encoding. Is the issue fixed?

options.text: No: encoding doesn't stop the wrong person receiving it
Yes: encoding hides the token from anyone reading the page
options.why: Encoding changes how text is shown, but the token is still delivered to the wrong person.

options.text: Yes: encoding prevents both disclosure and XSS at the same time
options.why: Encoding helps with XSS, but it doesn't stop a field being disclosed.

options.text: Only if the token is also moved into a cookie afterwards
options.why: Moving the token to a cookie still sends it to someone who shouldn't have it.

explanation: Disclosure is about which information is sent. Output encoding is about how untrusted text is represented. Review both.

prompt: Which of these are good practice for a security log? Select all that apply.

options.text: Record failed sign-ins, refused access and permission changes
Leave out passwords, access tokens and complete submitted forms
Restrict who can read the logs
Store the full request body for every sign-in
options.why: Full request bodies capture passwords and other secrets in the log.

options.text: Include the user's password to help debug lockouts
options.why: Logging passwords exposes them to anyone who can read the logs.

explanation: Select fields rather than recording whole forms. If secrets were already logged, deal with the retained copies and the exposed credentials too.

prompt: An endpoint checks ownership correctly but its serializer still returns an internal role flag. Which kind of authorisation failed?

options.text: Property-level
Object-level
options.why: Object-level access worked: the user may access this record. The problem is one field.

options.text: Function-level
options.why: Function-level is about which actions a user may perform, not which fields they see.

options.text: Authentication
options.why: The user is correctly identified; the failure is in which fields are returned.

explanation: Object-level asks whether you may access the record. Property-level asks which fields you may read or change.

prompt: A required API key is missing from configuration at startup. What should the application do?

options.text: Stop safely and report that the key is missing
Fall back to a known shared credential
options.why: A shared fallback credential is a known secret and weakens security.

options.text: Use a default key from the source code
options.why: Keys in source code end up in repositories and copies.

options.text: Continue and log the missing key's expected value
options.why: Logging the expected key would put a secret into the logs.

explanation: Keep real keys in protected server configuration or a secret store, give each only the permissions it needs, and support replacing them.

prompt: A sensitive value in an API response is exposed even if the page never displays it.
explanation: A sensitive value does not become safe because the interface ignores it. Equally, an unnecessary public field is not automatically a vulnerability: check sensitivity, permission and purpose.

prompt: Order the layers a piece of data passes through on its way from storage to the recipient.
explanation: Disclosure can happen at any layer, including headers, downloads and caches.

prompt: What is the term for refusing a protected action when the permission check cannot be completed?
explanation: An unavailable checking service has not granted permission. Failing open would turn a technical failure into unauthorised disclosure.

prompt: Different sign-in error messages let someone work out which email addresses have accounts. What is this called?
explanation: Return comparable responses, and do comparable work, for comparable failures.
